claim: DNA has proven to be a versatile molecular scaffold to build an array of programmable synthetic nanoarchitectures due to its structural predictability.
source: DNA has proven to be a versatile molecular scaffold to build an array of programmable synthetic nanoarchitectures due to its structural predictability (Seeman and Sleiman, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Seeman and Sleiman, 2017

claim: The specificity of Watson–Crick–Franklin base pairing, its tunable affinity, the well-defined structural properties of the double helix, and its modular nature make the DNA scaffold highly engineerable.
source: The specificity of Watson–Crick–Franklin base pairing, its tunable affinity, the well-defined structural properties of the double helix, and its modular nature make the DNA scaffold highly engineerable.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about DNA properties

claim: A wide array of functional DNA-based nanodevices have been deployed in vivo both for quantitative chemical imaging and also as programmable carriers that deliver encapsulated cargo upon receipt of a molecular cue.
source: A wide array of functional DNA-based nanodevices have been deployed in vivo both for quantitative chemical imaging and also as programmable carriers that deliver encapsulated cargo upon receipt of a molecular cue (Chakraborty et al., 2017; Chakraborty et al., 2016; Jani et al., 2020; Krishnan and Bathe, 2012; Lee et al., 2012; Li et al., 2011; Modi et al., 2009; Narayanaswamy et al., 2019; Saha et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2014; Surana et al., 2011; Thekkan et al., 2019; Veetil et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: In most contexts, the site for payload action ideally needs to be confined to the desired organ or tissue.
source: However, in most contexts, the site for payload action ideally needs to be confined to the desired organ or tissue.
evidence: Based on general principles of targeted therapy

claim: DNA nanostructures are particularly amenable to endosomal trafficking.
source: DNA nanostructures are particularly amenable to endosomal trafficking, which has in part led to an array of synthetic DNA nanostructures being presently deployed in living systems (Bujold et al., 2018; Chakraborty et al., 2016; Krishnan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Endosomal trafficking is ubiquitous and regulates the internalization, sorting, and intracellular transport of diverse cargo.
source: Endosomal trafficking is ubiquitous: it regulates the internalization, sorting, and intracellular transport of diverse cargo, and is pivotal to development, signaling, and homeostasis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cellular biology

claim: Perturbations in endosomal trafficking are linked to multiple diseases, including neurodegeneration, cancer, and cardiovascular disease.
source: The significance and impact of endocytosis in health and disease is underscored by the observation that perturbations in endosomal trafficking are linked to multiple diseases, including neurodegeneration, cancer, and cardiovascular disease, and further, distinct cell types differ in their susceptibility to disease (Maxfield, 2014; Mellman and Yarden, 2013; Mukherjee et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maxfield, 2014; Mellman and Yarden, 2013; Mukherjee et al., 1997

claim: DNA nanodevices can be targeted tissue-specifically and with organelle-level precision in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: By leveraging membrane trafficking as well as taking advantage of biological barriers present in the whole organism, we show that DNA nanodevices can be targeted tissue-specifically and with organelle-level precision in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
evidence: This is the main claim of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript

claim: Most studies that use DNA nanostructures as reporters or payload carriers describe their functionality primarily in cultured cells that express scavenger receptors for which DNA is the natural ligand.
source: Most studies that use DNA nanostructures as reporters or payload carriers describe their functionality primarily in cultured cells that express scavenger receptors for which DNA is the natural ligand (Li et al., 2011; Modi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2011; Modi et al., 2009

claim: In vivo studies in multicellular organisms have exploited scavenger receptor-mediated endocytosis to target DNA architectures to phagocytic cells such as coelomocytes in C. elegans or microglia in Danio rerio.
source: In vivo studies in multicellular organisms have also exploited scavenger receptor-mediated endocytosis to target DNA architectures to phagocytic cells such as coelomocytes in C. elegans (Surana et al., 2011) or microglia in Danio rerio (Veetil et al., 2020; Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1a

claim: Most cells and tissues do not endogenously express scavenger receptors.
source: However, since most cells and tissues do not endogenously express scavenger receptors, targeting DNA nanostructures to such cell types in vivo remains challenging.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of scavenger receptor expression patterns

claim: In cultured cells, DNA nanodevices can be targeted by chemically conjugating a natural ligand to the nanodevice, which then binds its cognate receptor on the cell surface and gets internalized.
source: In cultured cells, this problem is circumvented by exploiting naturally occurring receptor-ligand interactions. The natural ligand is chemically conjugated to a DNA nanodevice, which then binds its cognate receptor on the cell surface and gets internalized and transported within the cell along the trafficking route adopted by the receptor (Bhatia et al., 2016; Jani et al., 2020; Modi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhatia et al., 2016; Jani et al., 2020; Modi et al., 2013

claim: A synthetic receptor-ligand interaction has been used where the receptor is a sequence-specific, DNA-binding protein based on a single-chain variable fragment (scFv).
source: Alternately, a synthetic receptor-ligand interaction has been used where the receptor is a sequence-specific, DNA-binding protein based on a single-chain variable fragment (scFv) (Modi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Modi et al., 2013

claim: When an scFv is fused to a trafficking protein such as furin and the chimera is expressed in cells, furin displays the synthetic scFv receptor on the cell surface.
source: When the scFv is fused to a trafficking protein such as furin, and the chimera is expressed in cells, furin displays the synthetic scFv receptor on the cell surface.
evidence: Supported by citation to Modi et al., 2013

claim: DNA nanodevices with an scFv-binding sequence engage the scFv domain of the chimera and get trafficked to specific organelles within the cell.
source: Thus, DNA nanodevices with an scFv-binding sequence engage the scFv domain of the chimera and get trafficked to specific organelles within the cell (Modi et al., 2013; Saminathan et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Modi et al., 2013; Saminathan et al., 2021

claim: There is no evidence that DNA nanostructures can be targeted to tissues lacking scavenger receptors in multicellular organisms.
source: Despite these in cellulo demonstrations, there is still no evidence that DNA nanostructures can be targeted to tissues lacking scavenger receptors in multicellular organisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study

claim: DNA nanodevices can be targeted tissue-specifically in the nematode C. elegans by leveraging both natural and synthetic receptors on the surface of different cell types.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that DNA nanodevices can be targeted tissue-specifically in the nematode C. elegans by leveraging both natural and synthetic receptors on the surface of different cell types.
evidence: This is a main claim of the study, supported by experimental data

claim: The intestine is one of the major organs of C. elegans, comprising a third of the total somatic mass with 20 large epithelial cells positioned with bilateral symmetry.
source: The intestine is one of the major organs of C. elegans, comprising a third of the total somatic mass with 20 large epithelial cells positioned with bilateral symmetry, forming a long tube around a lumen (Altun and Hall, 2009; McGhee, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Altun and Hall, 2009; McGhee, 2007

claim: IECs contain prominent, birefringent gut granules that are known as lysosome-related organelles (LROs).
source: IECs contain prominent, birefringent gut granules that are known as lysosome-related organelles (LROs).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of C. elegans intestinal cell biology

claim: LROs are distinguished by lysosomal markers.
source: Distinguished by lysosomal markers (Coburn and Gems, 2013; Dell'Angelica et al., 2000; Hermann et al., 2005), LROs play important roles in production and storage of melanin, immune defense, and neurological function (Huizing et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coburn and Gems, 2013; Dell'Angelica et al., 2000; Hermann et al., 2005

claim: LROs play important roles in production and storage of melanin, immune defense, and neurological function.
source: Distinguished by lysosomal markers (Coburn and Gems, 2013; Dell'Angelica et al., 2000; Hermann et al., 2005), LROs play important roles in production and storage of melanin, immune defense, and neurological function (Huizing et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huizing et al., 2008

claim: The biological barrier between the intestinal lumen and the pseudocoelom effectively precludes D38 from access to coelomocytes.
source: We reasoned that the biological barrier between the intestinal lumen and the pseudocoelom would effectively preclude D38 from access to coelomocytes, as seen whenever DNA nanodevices are microinjected in the pseudocoelom (Bhatia et al., 2011; Surana et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on inference from prior observations cited in Bhatia et al., 2011; Surana et al., 2011

claim: The mean intensity corresponding to D38 uptake in IECs, compared to control mock-fed worms, was very low, indicating low or no intrinsic targetability of DNA nanodevices to IECs.
source: The mean intensity corresponding to D38 uptake, compared to control mock-fed worms, was very low, indicating low or no intrinsic targetability of DNA nanodevices to IECs (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a,b

claim: Increasing the number of base pairs and/or negative charges in DNA nanodevices (D50 or D100) did not improve targeting to IECs.
source: Using the same liquid-feeding method, we repeated uptake experiments with 50- or 100-bp-long dsDNA (D50 or D100). Again, there was no enhancement in nanodevice targeting to IECs (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a

claim: DNA nanostructures are not inherently targeted to intestinal epithelial cells.
source: This revealed that DNA nanostructures are not inherently targeted to cells in this tissue.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data on D38, D50, and D100 uptake

claim: Worms are capable of endocytosing dsRNA localized in the acidic intestinal lumen, and this is effected by the membrane protein SID-2.
source: Previous studies have shown that worms are capable of endocytosing dsRNA localized in the acidic intestinal lumen, and that this is effected by the membrane protein SID-2 (Hunter et al., 2006; McEwan et al., 2012; Winston et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hunter et al., 2006; McEwan et al., 2012; Winston et al., 2007

claim: When worms were liquid-fed either R100 or R50, uptake efficiency by intestinal epithelia increased approximately two fold compared to their DNA analogues.
source: Interestingly, when worms were liquid-fed either R100 or R50 we observed that uptake efficiency by intestinal epithelia increased approximately two fold compared to their DNA analogues (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: Conjugating R100 to DNA nanodevices improved uptake of the latter by IECs.
source: When nematodes were liquid-fed the above chimeras and then imaged, we found that overall conjugating R100 to DNA nanodevices improved uptake of the latter by IECs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on R100Dn chimeras

claim: The length of the dsDNA scaffold had no significant effect on uptake efficiency of R100Dn chimeras.
source: However, interestingly, we observed that the length of the dsDNA scaffold had no significant effect on uptake efficiency (Figure 2d,e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d,e

claim: It is possible to target DNA nanodevices to IECs using a DNA-RNA chimera.
source: Thus, it is possible to target DNA nanodevices to IECs using a DNA-RNA chimera.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data on R100Dn chimeras

claim: R50Dn nanodevices internalized by intestinal epithelia localized to LROs.
source: Closer scrutiny revealed that R50Dn nanodevices internalized by intestinal epithelia localized to LROs, readily identified by their high autofluorescence at low wavelengths (Soukas et al., 2013), as well as colocalization with LAMP-1::GFP and GLO::1-GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Schroeder et al., 2007; Soukas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations

claim: Uptake of R100D50 was reduced in sid-2&dyf-2 mutants, but not in sid-1(qt9), dyf-2(gk678), or wild-type worms.
source: We found that uptake was reduced in sid-2&dyf-2 mutants, but not in sid-1(qt9), dyf-2(gk678), or wild-type worms.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing uptake in different genetic backgrounds

claim: SID-2 is localized on the extracellular surface, acting as a receptor that binds and endocytoses dsRNA.
source: Our results are consistent with SID-2 being localized on the extracellular surface, acting as a receptor that binds and endocytoses dsRNA, while SID-1 is resident in endosomes, where it binds dsRNA cargo and transports it into the cytosol (Jose and Hunter, 2007; Li et al., 2015; McEwan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jose and Hunter, 2007; Li et al., 2015; McEwan et al., 2012

claim: SID-1 is resident in endosomes, where it binds dsRNA cargo and transports it into the cytosol.
source: Our results are consistent with SID-2 being localized on the extracellular surface, acting as a receptor that binds and endocytoses dsRNA, while SID-1 is resident in endosomes, where it binds dsRNA cargo and transports it into the cytosol (Jose and Hunter, 2007; Li et al., 2015; McEwan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jose and Hunter, 2007; Li et al., 2015; McEwan et al., 2012

claim: SID-2 is the receptor for nanodevice internalization and its subsequent trafficking to LROs in IECs.
source: This implicates SID-2 as the receptor for nanodevice internalization and its subsequent trafficking to LROs in IECs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genetic experiments showing sid-2 dependence

claim: C. elegans has proven to be a powerful model organism to study vesicular trafficking in neurons, given its transparent body and simple nervous system.
source: C. elegans has proven to be a powerful model organism to study vesicular trafficking in neurons, given its transparent body and simple nervous system (Hulme and Whitesides, 2011; Teschendorf and Link, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hulme and Whitesides, 2011; Teschendorf and Link, 2009

claim: Neurons do not express either scavenger receptors or SID proteins.
source: However, neurons do not express either scavenger receptors or SID proteins, complicating the targeting of DNA nanodevices to these cell types.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of neuronal receptor expression

claim: Humanized VHH antibodies lack a light chain altogether, and the heavy chain itself is sufficient to form the antigen-binding pocket.
source: Humanized VHH antibodies lack a light chain altogether, and the heavy chain itself is sufficient to form the antigen-binding pocket (Hamers et al., 1993), leading to their utility in therapeutics as well as cell biology (Harmsen and De Haard, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hamers et al., 1993; Harmsen and De Haard, 2007

claim: VHH antibodies robustly maintain their native conformations due to increased hydrophilicity and single-domain nature and are much more resistant to thermal and chemical denaturation.
source: They robustly maintain their native conformations due to increased hydrophilicity and single-domain nature and are much more resistant to thermal and chemical denaturation (Dumoulin et al., 2002; Ewert et al., 2002; Pérez et al., 2001; van der Linden et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dumoulin et al., 2002; Ewert et al., 2002; Pérez et al., 2001; van der Linden et al., 1999

claim: Nearly 70% of the 160 randomly selected clones displayed DNA-binding properties.
source: Nearly 70% displayed DNA-binding properties, of which 40 bound DNA regardless of whether it was double- or single-stranded.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from phage display screen

claim: 42 VHH clones were found to show sequence specificity for the dsDNA target and showed minimal binding to ssDNA of the same sequence or dsDNA with a different sequence.
source: Interestingly, 42 were found to show sequence specificity for the dsDNA target and showed minimal binding to ssDNA of the same sequence or dsDNA with a different sequence.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from phage display screen

claim: Nearly 80% of the 42 dsDNA-binding VHH antibodies specifically bound region R1.
source: Of the 42-dsDNA-binding VHH antibodies tested, nearly 80% specifically bound region R1, albeit with varying affinities (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Each of the 42 VHH antibodies required only the first 4-bp at the 3′ end of region R1 (ATAA) for binding.
source: ELISAs revealed that each of the 42 VHH antibodies required only the first 4-bp at the 3′ end of region R1 (ATAA, nucleotides in red) for binding (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c

claim: When the 4-bp ATAA sequence is present not at the terminus, but in the middle of the dsDNA duplex, it was no longer a ligand for any of the 42 VHH antibodies.
source: When this 4-bp sequence is present not at the terminus, but in the middle of the dsDNA duplex, as in R6, it was no longer a ligand for any of the 42 VHH antibodies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on R6 construct

claim: The minimal binding epitope for all 42 VHH antibodies isolated was a terminal d(ATAA) motif.
source: This clearly demonstrated that the minimal binding epitope for all 42 VHH antibodies isolated was a terminal d(ATAA) motif (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data on various DNA constructs

claim: The VHH 9E demonstrated ~82% binding even at pH 5.
source: From a pH-dependent ELISA screen, we identified that the VHH 9E was disrupted the least by acidification, demonstrating ~82% binding even at pH 5 (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: The relative binding affinity of VHH 9E to its target epitope was ~200 nM.
source: Finally, based on ELISA, we estimated that the relative binding affinity of VHH 9E to its target epitope was ~200 nM (Figure 3e, Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e

claim: The recombinant, humanized VHH antibody 9E binds with high specificity to a 3′ terminal, d(ATAA) region.
source: Cumulatively, our findings show that the recombinant, humanized VHH antibody 9E binds with high specificity to a 3′ terminal, d(ATAA) region (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental characterizations

claim: Synaptobrevin-1 (SNB-1) is an integral membrane protein present in multiple copies in synaptic vesicles.
source: Our choice of synaptobrevin-1 as a carrier protein was guided by it being an integral membrane protein present in multiple copies in synaptic vesicles (Dittman and Ryan, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dittman and Ryan, 2009

claim: SNB-1 has a low molecular weight (~16 kDa).
source: It has a low molecular weight (~16 kDa) and its N-terminal cytoplasmic domain interacts with target membrane SNARE (t-SNARE) proteins to facilitate neurotransmitter exocytosis, while its C-terminus has a hydrophobic patch that anchors it to vesicular membranes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of SNB-1 structure

claim: The C-terminus of SNB-1 ends in a short tail that extends into the vesicular lumen and is exposed to the synaptic cleft during exocytosis.
source: The C-terminus ends in a short tail that extends into the vesicular lumen and is exposed to the synaptic cleft during exocytosis (Hanson et al., 1997; Südhof, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hanson et al., 1997; Südhof, 1995

claim: Upon their fusion with the plasma membrane at the synaptic cleft, synaptic vesicles undergo recycling via the endosomal pathway.
source: Upon their fusion with the plasma membrane at the synaptic cleft, synaptic vesicles undergo recycling via the endosomal pathway (Rizzoli, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rizzoli, 2014

claim: Fusing GFP (~27 kDa) to the C-terminus of SNB-1 does not perturb SNB-1 localization or function.
source: Furthermore, fusing GFP (~27 kDa) to the C-terminus of SNB-1 (Murthy et al., 2011; Nonet, 1999) does not perturb SNB-1 localization or function (Nonet, 1999; Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by citations to Murthy et al., 2011; Nonet, 1999

claim: Several punctate structures, linearly arranged along the worm's body strongly resembling neuronal synapses along the C. elegans dorsal and ventral nerve cords, were observed when nDA647N was injected into psnb-1::snb-1::9E worms.
source: We observed several punctate structures, linearly arranged along the worm's body strongly resembling neuronal synapses along the C. elegans dorsal and ventral nerve cords (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b

claim: When 500 nM nDA647N was injected into jsIs682 [rab-3p::GFP::rab-3 + lin-15(+)]; psnb-1::snb-1::9E worms, nDA647N labeling coincides with GFP::RAB-3, confirming synaptic labeling.
source: When 500 nM nDA647N was injected into jsIs682 [rab-3p::GFP::rab-3 + lin-15(+)]; psnb-1::snb-1::9E worms, we found that nDA647N labeling coincides with GFP::RAB-3, confirming synaptic labeling.
evidence: Supported by experimental colocalization data

claim: nDA647N containing puncta do not exclusively colocalize with GFP::RAB-3-positive puncta within the same axon.
source: Interestingly, nDA647N containing puncta do not exclusively colocalize with GFP::RAB-3-positive puncta within the same axon.
evidence: Supported by experimental colocalization data

claim: Line profiles for ROIs drawn perpendicular to long axis of different neurons revealed ~80% colocalization between nDA647N and GFP::RAB-3.
source: To evaluate colocalization, we plotted line profiles for ROIs drawn perpendicular to long axis of different neurons, which revealed ~80% colocalization (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: In addition to the synaptic regions of neurons, nDA647N might be labeling trafficking endosomal compartments or synaptic vesicles that are being recycled.
source: This suggests that in addition to the synaptic regions of neurons, nDA647N might be labeling trafficking endosomal compartments or synaptic vesicles that are being recycled.
evidence: Inference drawn from incomplete colocalization with synaptic markers

claim: DNA nanodevices are normally taken up by scavenger receptors present on coelomocytes when introduced into the pseudocoelom.
source: Normally when DNA nanodevices are introduced into the pseudocoelom, they are taken up by scavenger receptors present on coelomocytes (Chakraborty et al., 2017; Dan et al., 2019; Narayanaswamy et al., 2019; Surana et al., 2011; Veetil et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: Nanodevice uptake via scavenger receptors is easily abolished in the presence of 10 equivalent molar excess of maleylated BSA.
source: A key characteristic of nanodevice uptake via this pathway is that uptake is easily abolished in the presence of 10 equivalent molar excess of maleylated BSA as the latter competes for scavenger receptors due to its anionic nature (Haberland and Fogelman, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haberland and Fogelman, 1985

claim: Even in the presence of 10 equivalents excess of maleylated BSA, neuronal labeling of psnb-1::snb-1::9E worms with nDA647N was not affected.
source: Importantly, even in the presence of 10 equivalents excess of maleylated BSA, neuronal labeling of psnb-1::snb-1::9E worms with nDA647N was not affected (Figure 4c–i).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c-i

claim: nDA647N uptake into neurons does not occur via scavenger receptors.
source: This indicates that nDA647N uptake into neurons does not occur via scavenger receptors.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from maleylated BSA competition experiment

claim: When the terminal d(ATAA) motif in nDA647N was removed to give nD2A647, no neuronal labeling was observed.
source: When the terminal d(ATAA) motif in nDA647N was removed to give a DNA nanodevice denoted nD2A647, we observed no such neuronal labeling (Figure 4cii).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4cii

claim: DNA nanodevices can be targeted to neurons in worms only if the former incorporate a d(ATAA) motif and if the latter express the SNB-1::9E chimera in neurons.
source: These results show that DNA nanodevices can be targeted to neurons in worms only if the former incorporate a d(ATAA) motif and if the latter express the SNB-1::9E chimera in neurons.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with nDA647N and nD2A647

claim: Acetylcholine is the most broadly used neurotransmitter in the nematode nervous system.
source: We focused on the cholinergic subset of motor neurons since acetylcholine is the most broadly used neurotransmitter in the nematode nervous system (Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pereira et al., 2015

claim: Cholinergic motor neurons in the ventral nerve cord are divided into six classes: DA, DB, AS, VA, VB, and VC.
source: Cholinergic motor neurons in the ventral nerve cord are divided into six classes: DA, DB, AS, VA, VB, and VC (Kerk et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017

claim: The acetylcholine receptor subunit ACR-2 is expressed in four of the six classes of cholinergic motor neurons (DA, DB, VA, VB).
source: Since the acetylcholine receptor subunit ACR-2 is expressed in four of the six classes of cholinergic motor neurons (DA, DB, VA, VB), we used the acr-2 promoter region to target these subsets of neurons (Kratsios et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kratsios et al., 2011

claim: When nDA647N was introduced into the pseudocoelom of pacr-2::snb-1::9E nematodes, it localized in several, linearly arranged punctate structures resembling synapses and/or neuronal endosomes, around the mid-section of the worm body corresponding to the axons of the VA and VB neurons of the ventral nerve cord.
source: When nDA647N (1 µM) was introduced into the pseudocoelom of these nematodes, we observed that it localized in several, linearly arranged punctate structures resembling synapses and/or neuronal endosomes, around the mid-section of the worm body corresponding to the axons of the VA and VB neurons of the ventral nerve cord (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d

claim: No labeling with nDA647N was observed in the dorsal nerve cord of pacr-2::SNB-1::9E worms.
source: The DA and DB neurons extend their axons to the dorsal nerve cord and form synapse with dorsal muscle. However, we did not observe any labeling with nDA647N in the dorsal nerve cord of pacr-2::SNB-1::9E worms.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The strategy selectively labels VA and VB neurons over DA and DB classes of neurons.
source: Thus, our strategy selectively labels VA and VB neurons over DA and DB classes of neurons.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from selective labeling pattern

claim: Selective labeling of VA and VB neurons could arise from the differential cell-surface levels of SNB-1::9E in VA and VB neurons, or greater accessibility of their synapses to cargo in the pseudocoelom, or both.
source: Such selective labeling could arise from the differential cell-surface levels of SNB-1::9E in VA and VB neurons, or greater accessibility of their synapses to cargo in the pseudocoelom, or both.
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms for selective labeling

claim: GLR-4 protein is known to be expressed in the head neurons and the SAB, and DA9 neurons.
source: In order to target nDA647N to these neurons, we chose the promoter of the glutamate receptor family protein GLR-4 (Feng et al., 2006) since this protein is known to be expressed in the head neurons and the SAB, and DA9 neurons (Brockie et al., 2001; "glr-4 (gene) - WormBase: Nematode Information Resource, 2021; Hills et al., 2004; Kratsios et al., 2015; Rothaug et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple sources

claim: When nDA647N was introduced into the pseudocoelom of pglr-4::snb-1::9E nematodes, it localized in punctate structures arranged around the pharynx, corresponding to the putative synapses of head neurons expressing GLR-4, and ventral neuromuscular synapses belonging to the SAB neurons.
source: When nDA647N (1 µM) was introduced into the pseudocoelom of these nematodes, we observed that it localized in punctate structures arranged around the pharynx, corresponding to the putative synapses of head neurons expressing GLR-4, and ventral neuromuscular synapses belonging to the SAB neurons (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e

claim: The DA9 neurons at the tail of the worm did not show labeling with nDA647N in pglr-4::snb-1::9E worms.
source: Again, just as in the previous case of the DA and DB neurons, the DA9 neurons at the tail of the worm did not show labeling, revealing that this method led to the preferential labeling of SAB neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: DNA nanodevices can be targeted to synapses and/or trafficking endosomes of specific neuron types expressing SNB-1::9E.
source: Taken together, our results show that DNA nanodevices can be targeted to synapses and/or trafficking endosomes of specific neuron types expressing SNB-1::9E.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with different promoters

claim: ODR-2 is a GPI-anchored, membrane-associated signaling protein that plays important roles in nematode chemotaxis.
source: ODR-2 is a GPI-anchored, membrane-associated signaling protein that plays important roles in nematode chemotaxis (Chou et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chou et al., 2001

claim: ODR-2 is highly expressed in sensory neurons, motor neurons, and interneurons, and is particularly enriched in axons.
source: ODR-2 is highly expressed in sensory neurons, motor neurons, and interneurons, and is particularly enriched in axons (Gottschalk and Schafer, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gottschalk and Schafer, 2006

claim: When psnb-1::odr-2::9E transgenics were injected with nDA647N, the DNA nanodevice labels neuronal axons corresponding to the ventral and the dorsal nerve cords.
source: When these transgenics were injected with nDA647N (1 µM), we observed that in all worms the DNA nanodevice labels neuronal axons corresponding to the ventral and the dorsal nerve cords (Figure 4f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f

claim: In psnb-1::odr-2::9E transgenics, a near-uniform pattern of plasma membrane labeling was observed that is reminiscent of ODR-2 staining.
source: In these transgenics, a near-uniform pattern of plasma membrane labeling was observed that is reminiscent of ODR-2 staining (Chou et al., 2001), and is in stark contrast to the punctate labeling that was observed in psnb-1::snb-1::9E worms (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and comparison to prior work

claim: The synthetic receptor-ligand strategy is generalizable to cell-surface membrane proteins and can be used to label specific membrane domains and/or endosomal compartments across neurons in vivo.
source: Taken together, our experiments show that the synthetic receptor-ligand strategy shown here is generalizable to cell-surface membrane proteins and can be used to label specific membrane domains and/or endosomal compartments across neurons in vivo.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with SNB-1 and ODR-2 fusions

claim: This design is applicable to a range of functional DNA nanostructures provided they harbor a d(ATAA) tag.
source: Additionally, this design is applicable to a range of functional DNA nanostructures provided they harbor a d(ATAA) tag, opening up new avenues for the cell-specific application of DNA nanodevices in biological systems.
evidence: Inference about the generalizability of the approach

claim: pHlava-9E is designed to provide a digital output of compartmentalization.
source: pHlava-9E is designed to provide a digital output of compartmentalization, that is, its pH profile is such that even if it is internalized into a mildly acidic vesicle, the pH readout is as high as one would observe with a lysosome.
evidence: Description of the design principle of pHlava-9E

claim: The in vitro pH performance curve of pHlava-9E shows a maximum fold change in O/R of 2.5 from pH 8 to pH 6.
source: The in vitro pH performance curve of pHlava-9E shows a maximum fold change in O/R of 2.5 from pH 8 to pH 6, indicating that pHlava-9E is particularly accurate to measure neutral or near neutral pH and well positioned to measure pH between pH 6 and 8 (Figure 5f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f

claim: pHlava-9E is designed such that any compartments with acidities ranging from pH 4 to 6 will all show the maximum O/R ratio.
source: It is also designed such that any compartments with acidities ranging from pH 4 to 6 will all show the maximum O/R ratio.
evidence: Description of the design principle of pHlava-9E

claim: The O/R ratio obtained in psnb-1::odr-2::9E worm neurons was 0.65 ± 0.03, corresponding to a pH of 7.2.
source: In line with our expectations, the O/R ratio obtained, as revealed from the fold change in signal with respect to that in lysosomes, was 0.65 ± 0.03, corresponding to a pH of 7.2 (Figure 5b,d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b,d

claim: The O/R value of the punctate structures in pHlava-9E labeled neurons of psnb-1::snb-1::9E worms was 0.99 ± 0.03.
source: The O/R value of the punctate structures in pHlava-9E labeled neurons of psnb-1::snb-1::9E worms was 0.99 ± 0.03 (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c,d

claim: The O/R ratios obtained from coelomocytes in psnb-1::snb-1::9E worms injected with pHlava-9E corresponded to the maximum possible value of 0.99 ± 0.03 reported by this device.
source: As expected, the O/R ratios obtained corresponded to the maximum possible value of 0.99 ± 0.03 reported by this device (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d

claim: Minimally 93% of pHlava-9E is present in compartments in the neurons of psnb-1::snb-1::9E worms.
source: Based on the comparison of values obtained from the neurons of psnb-1::snb-1::9E worms, maximally 7% of nanodevice could still be on the plasma membrane without nudging the O/R value beyond the experimental error (0.03) (Figure 5f). This indicates that minimally 93% of pHlava-9E is present in compartments in the neurons of psnb-1::snb-1::9E worms.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from pH measurements and calibration

claim: Endocytosis and endosome trafficking are complex processes, regulating many critical cellular functions and therefore play pivotal roles in tissue-specific physiology and pathology.
source: Endocytosis and endosome trafficking are complex processes, regulating many critical cellular functions and therefore play pivotal roles in tissue-specific physiology and pathology.

source: Our knowledge of subcellular dynamics and organization of endocytic and recycling pathways stems largely from investigations in cultured cellular systems.

claim: In vivo, endocytosis in single cells and their functional outcomes are sculpted by molecular interactions with their neighboring cells, occurring in the presence of multiple biochemical cues originating from other tissues.

claim: Simply introducing DNA nanodevices into the worm intestine and circumventing the relevant biological barrier does not lead to nanodevice targeting to IECs.
source: Our results show that, unlike what has been observed for coelomocytes (Chakraborty et al., 2017; Dan et al., 2019; Narayanaswamy et al., 2019; Surana et al., 2011; Veetil et al., 2017), simply introducing DNA nanodevices into the worm intestine and circumventing the relevant biological barrier does not lead to nanodevice targeting to IECs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data on D38, D50, D100 uptake

claim: By exploiting the endogenous dsRNA receptor SID-2 in IECs, DNA nanodevices can be targeted to these cells.
source: However, by exploiting the endogenous dsRNA receptor SID-2 in IECs, we could target DNA nanodevices to these cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data on R100Dn chimeras

claim: By conjugating a dsRNA domain to DNA nanodevices, the dsRNA domain engaged the SID-2 receptor such that the DNA nanodevice underwent receptor-mediated endocytosis and was subsequently trafficked to LROs.
source: We achieved this by conjugating a dsRNA domain to DNA nanodevices, where the dsRNA domain engaged the SID-2 receptor such that the DNA nanodevice underwent receptor-mediated endocytosis and was subsequently trafficked to LROs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data on R100Dn chimeras and colocalization studies

claim: Mutations in the sid-2 gene, but not sid-1, abrogated DNA nanodevice uptake.
source: Furthermore, since mutations in the sid-2 gene, but not sid-1, abrogated DNA nanodevice uptake, we could pinpoint that nanodevice targeting occurs via the endogenous SID-2 receptor.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing uptake in different genetic backgrounds

claim: DNA nanodevices can be targeted tissue-specifically by exploiting relevant endogenously expressed cell-surface receptors and displaying the cognate ligand on the DNA nanodevice.
source: Our results show that DNA nanodevices can be targeted tissue-specifically by exploiting relevant endogenously expressed cell-surface receptors and displaying the cognate ligand on the DNA nanodevice.

claim: 9E binds a specific 4-nt sequence, namely d(ATAA), when it is present at the 3′ end of the DNA nanodevice with high affinity (~200 nM), irrespective of the environmental pH.
source: We therefore identified a sequence-specific, DNA-binding recombinant humanized VHH antibody, denoted 9E, by phage display. 9E binds a specific 4-nt sequence, namely d(ATAA), when it is present at the 3′ end of the DNA nanodevice with high affinity (~200 nM), irrespective of the environmental pH.
evidence: Supported by experimental characterization of 9E

claim: By fusing 9E to proteins that are expressed on the target cell under appropriate tissue-specific promoters, DNA nanodevices can be targeted with cellular- and subcellular-level precision.
source: By fusing 9E to proteins that are expressed on the target cell under appropriate tissue-specific promoters, we can target DNA nanodevices with cellular- and subcellular-level precision.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with SNB-1::9E and ODR-2::9E

claim: SNB-1 is ubiquitously expressed in all neurons.
source: For example, since SNB-1 is ubiquitously expressed in all neurons, we expressed a SNB-1::9E fusion protein under the pan-neuronal promoter psnb-1 and targeted a DNA nanodevice displaying the 3′ terminal d(ATAA) sequence, specifically to neurons.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of SNB-1 expression

claim: Nanodevices labeled endosomes not only at the synapses but all along the axon within the relevant neurons.
source: Interestingly, nanodevices labeled endosomes not only at the synapses but all along the axon within the relevant neurons.
